rawIngestions.titleRaw: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
rawIngestions.contentRaw: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

payloadJson.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution

rawIngestions.titleRaw: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
rawIngestions.contentRaw:
An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private.
  We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations.
  We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.

payloadJson.title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering

rawIngestions.titleRaw: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
rawIngestions.contentRaw:
The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions.
  This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

payloadJson.title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations

rawIngestions.titleRaw: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
rawIngestions.contentRaw: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

payloadJson.title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers

rawIngestions.titleRaw: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model
rawIngestions.contentRaw: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.

payloadJson.title: Adaptive Scenario Generation for KL-DRO Around a Learned Density Model

rawIngestions.titleRaw: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application
rawIngestions.contentRaw: Luggage re-identification (ReID) is a critical task in video surveillance for forensics, security or border management (suspicious or abandoned luggage recognition), as well as luggage management (lost luggage recovery). It enables the association of observations of the same luggage across disjoint camera views in complex environments such as airports, train stations and border crossing. While existing approaches primarily focus on appearance-based cropped image matching under relatively clean conditions, real-world scenarios are characterized by frequent occlusions, cluttered background and crowded scenes which significantly degrade performance. Yet, strategies leveraging the complementarity of multiple shots and views from different video streams is overlooked. In this paper, we study strategies for an end-to-end pipeline that operates from multiple video streams to detect and re-identify luggage. We evaluate different variants on a benchmark dataset acquired in real-world environments to address the questions of selecting and merging different views and shots of the same luggage as well as training on different environment datasets for an overall ReID performance improvement in practical applications.

payloadJson.title: Luggage re-identification: A study of strategies towards a real-world application

rawIngestions.contentRaw:

- Added `permissions.blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories`: Write, Edit and NotebookEdit refuse paths outside the working directories in every permission mode
- Added an optional `groups` list to Claude apps gateway upstreams: only developers in the listed IdP groups are sent to that upstream, on failover too

- Added idle compaction to VS Code and Claude Desktop's Code tab: a 200K+ token conversation left idle is summarized, and the summary is used on your next message if the prompt cache has expired
- Fixed sessions failing turn after turn with "Invalid effort level" when an organization's admin caps a model's effort: Claude Code now lowers the effort, retries, and says which level it uses
- Fixed `claude -p` exiting with code 0 and no output when startup failed; it now prints the error and exits 1
- Fixed Bedrock sessions with many images failing every turn and `/compact` with "400 Input is too long." instead of removing older images and compacting
- Fixed Microsoft Foundry sessions failing when the resource has no deployment for the default Sonnet, Opus or Haiku model: Claude Code now falls back to an older model of that family
- Fixed repeated refused requests behind a gateway that doesn't accept tool search's `tool_reference` blocks: the request is sent again once without tool search, and the session remembers
- Fixed TLS connections failing with `UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT` when the system certificate store holds a renewed root certificate that is cross-signed with its predecessor
- Fixed MCP servers that also work without sign-in showing "needs authentication" after their stored sign-in stopped working; they are now used signed out

- Changed `/ultrareview` to check workspace trust before it runs git, as `claude ultrareview` does
- Changed the Bash tool's shell to clear any inherited `which` alias or function and to stop passing exported `which`/`unsetenv` functions to commands, so `which` is the system command or zsh builtin
- Changed `/permissions` Recently blocked to refuse approving a call you can't read in full, including one the terminal is too short to show

- Changed hook `if` conditions such as `Monitor(tail *)` to match the Monitor tool's shell commands as `Bash(tail *)` matches Bash's

- [VSCode] Fixed missing spinner and Stop button while a queued message's hooks run
- [VSCode] Fixed session group changes that cannot be saved, such as a delete, failing silently; an error notification now appears
- [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+F / Ctrl+F not opening the find widget in the plan preview tab
- [VSCode] Fixed the voice dictation shortcut (Ctrl+D) doing nothing under non-Latin keyboard layouts such as Russian, Greek or Hebrew
- [VSCode] Fixed missed one-time saved scheduled tasks being deleted without asking when the extension opened without a chat
- [VSCode] Changed `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CFC_PROMPT` to also stop the extension adding the Claude in Chrome instructions to a session's messages; the browser tools stay available
- [Cloud sessions] Added an Include completed button to the Scheduled tasks page when finished one-off tasks are the only ones hidden, so you can show them without opening the Sort menu
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed recently used self-hosted environments never appearing among the recent environments on the new session card
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud sessions reporting uncommitted changes every turn after Claude moved a branch to a commit it had pushed from another worktree
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed the self-hosted environment details dialog in admin settings squeezing its content out of view in very short windows or at high zoom; the dialog now scrolls
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed the permission mode picker staying on Auto after a running cloud or Remote Control session refused the switch; it now shows the mode in use and tells you

- [Cloud sessions] Improved Test connection for GitHub Enterprise in admin settings to also connect the way cloud sessions do, and to warn you when that second test fails

rawIngestions.contentRaw:
## What's changed

- Added `oidc.user_id_claim` to the Claude apps gateway, to identify people by an id_token claim other than `sub`, such as Microsoft Entra ID's `oid`
- Added click to send: in fullscreen, clicking the "to send now" hint under a queued message sends it right away, as its key does
- Fixed managed settings and organization policy not being fetched for the rest of the session after signing in from the VS Code extension
- Fixed Claude overwriting a very large CLAUDE.md, rules file or @-included file in a subdirectory after seeing only its start; Write now asks Claude to read it all or edit in place
- Fixed per-directory and `paths:` skills not being found after a Bash `cd` deeper into a git repository
- Fixed a rare case where the first reply after resuming a session in the terminal could be missing the next time the session was resumed
- Fixed a command with an invalid name stopping all commands from loading, which could leave `claude -p` with no output
- Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
- Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry `effort` values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force
- Fixed the `/model` and `/effort` cache warning saying the re-read waits for your next message; a change made while Claude is working can trigger it sooner
- Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
- Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
- Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty `!` input
- Fixed vim mode `d`, `c` and `y` with a `gj` or `gk` count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
- Fixed `/verify` showing a long description meant for Claude in `/help` and the `/` command menu instead of a short one
- Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
- Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
- Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set `CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0` to keep the full prompt
- Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1` to turn them off
- Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
- Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
- Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a `timeout` under 1 second now counts as 1 second
- Changed a subagent's `autoCompactWindow` to lower the window set by `CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW`, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
- Changed OpenTelemetry `mcp_server.name` to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of `custom`
- Changed Claude Code to stop sending the `claude_code.safety_event` OpenTelemetry event
- [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
- [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
- [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
- [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
- [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
- [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
- [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
- [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
- [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
- [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
- [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
- [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit

## What's changed

- Added `--hold-idle-file` and `--max-hold-min` to `self-hosted-runner`, to keep an idle session while your host reports processes it left running
- Added a tip for the Explanatory output style, shown when you ask Claude for explanations
- Fixed long freezes at startup and after reading or editing files when a CLAUDE.md file holds a very long list item
- Fixed interrupting Claude not taking effect until a timeout while an MCP server had not answered a resource read or a skill was still downloading
- Fixed standard-context sessions stopping with "Usage credits required for 1M context" when a request ran over 200K tokens; Claude Code now compacts the conversation and continues
- Fixed Write and Edit stalling for up to 5 seconds after they ran, and reporting 0 lines changed, when changing thousands of lines in a file
- Fixed subagents being unable to use MCP tools from servers that finish connecting after the subagent starts
- Fixed Claude seeing stale MEMORY.md and CLAUDE.md content right after automatic compaction when those files were edited earlier in the session
- Fixed `claude -p` and SDK sessions saving transcript messages out of order or keeping messages that were taken back
- Fixed `SubagentStop` hooks running about twice a minute for each running subagent instead of once when it finishes
- Fixed the @ file picker ignoring `.ignore`/`.rgignore` negation rules that re-include git-ignored files
- Fixed a subagent's isolated worktree being removed while a background subagent it started was still working in it
- Fixed background agents in auto mode that wait on their own shells starting a new main conversation turn on every wake
- Fixed the Bash tool description claiming the working directory always persists between calls
- Fixed the environment block naming a shell commands don't run in, such as fish when the Bash tool uses zsh
- Fixed `claude mcp add`, `claude mcp remove` and `/mcp` naming the current folder instead of the project entry in `~/.claude.json` that holds a local-scope server when run below a repository root
- Fixed `claude mcp list` and `claude mcp get` showing the error code twice on failed-connection lines (for example `ENOENT: ENOENT: …`)
- Fixed Remote Control sessions staying on "Connecting" for about two minutes when a network proxy blocks a startup request
- Fixed messages that Claude sends to a cloud or Remote Control session appearing as your own message in the Claude mobile apps
- Fixed Claude not being told the cause when a file attached to a message sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session could not be saved because the disk was full, or that a message's attachments past the first 20 were left out
- Fixed WebFetch and WebSearch hanging on a stalled response in Cowork cloud sessions; an unfinished request now fails after 300 seconds
- Fixed a background session that crashed between turns not being restarted while it was attached, pinned, or had a scheduled task or wake-up set
- Fixed the "background service did not respond" error suggesting the disabled `claude daemon restart`; it now suggests `claude daemon stop --any` and says it ends background sessions
- Fixed `claude respawn <id>` starting the background service before reporting that no background session matches the id
- Fixed `/effort` not warning about a prompt cache miss in plan mode when the plan model differs from the session model
- Fixed `/ide` saying the VS Code extension was installed before the install finished or when it failed
- Fixed the Write tool's file preview skipping rows and miscounting hidden lines when a line is wider than the terminal
- Fixed ↑ in an agent's chat tab recalling a message that was still waiting to be delivered, so resending it sent a second copy
- Fixed Cowork cloud sessions losing their connectors and most tools after a restart when a plugin or your settings named an `agent`; Cowork cloud sessions now ignore that setting
- Fixed agent teams sessions showing an empty task list when coming back with `--resume`, `--continue`, `/resume` or `--session-id`, including after `/clear` or a crash, and `/branch` writing to the original session's list
- Fixed pasting text that mentions an image file, such as `! open /tmp/shot.png` or `/review look at /tmp/shot.png`, attaching the image and dropping its path from the prompt
- Fixed the feedback draft card showing its 1/2/0 and Esc shortcuts while the prompt has text, when those keys act on the prompt instead of the card

- Fixed compaction after a "Prompt is too long" error keeping too much of a conversation with dense text, such as base64 or SVG, so the next request could fail again
- Fixed file read permission prompts not showing where a symbolic link leads
- Fixed a question's auto-continue timeout firing the moment the external editor closed after a long edit
- Windows: Fixed PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks letting a tool call through when Git Bash is missing and the hook's command is only quoted strings, such as a quoted path

- Improved memory use of non-interactive sessions (`-p`, Agent SDK) during compaction when the transcript file is very large
- Improved a mod's `Image` to draw inside tmux with `allow-passthrough` and `focus-events` on, in kitty, Ghostty, and iTerm2 3.5+ with fullscreen rendering, where it showed only its `alt` text

rawIngestions.contentRaw: ## New Models ### Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's largest and most capable model to date: a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 49 billion active parameters per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own datacenters in Europe. Mistral Large 4 unifies instruction following, reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows in a single set of weights. While a generalist model, it shows especially good performance on workloads such as cybersecurity, finance, and law, and it surpasses frontier closed models on visual grounding. It is natively fluent in 160+ languages, including every official language of the European Union. #### Key Features Mistral Large 4 includes the following architectural choices: - **~1T total / ~52B active parameters**: granular Mixture-of-Experts with 128 routed experts (4 active per token) and 1 shared expert. - **1M context length**, for long-context workloads. - **Multimodal input**: accepts text and image input, with text output. Pixtral-style vision encoder trained to handle variable image sizes and aspect ratios. - **Instruct and Reasoning functionalities** with function calls, reasoning effort configurable per request. Mistral Large 4 offers the following capabilities: - **Reasoning Mode**: three reasoning efforts — `low`, `medium`, `high` (default) — so the same model can answer a quick chat reply or work through a complex agentic run. - **Vision**: analyzes images, charts, technical drawings, and documents, with state-of-the-art visual grounding among open weights. - **Multilingual**: natively fluent in 160+ languages, including all official languages of the European Union. - **System Prompt**: strong adherence and support for system prompts. - **Agentic**: native function calling, JSON output, and strict JSON schema enforcement. - **Cybersecurity**: state of the art among open-weight models for security work, while refusing malicious requests. - **Large Context Window**: supports a 1M context window. The model is released under the [**Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License**](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B/blob/main/LICENSE): a modified version of the MIT license, for both commercial and non-commercial use — operating a Model-as-a-Service business requires a separate commercial license with Mistral. #### Recommended Settings - **Reasoning Effort**: - `'low'` / `'medium'` / `'high'` — default is `'high'`. - Use `reasoning_effort="high"` for complex prompts and agentic usage, `'low'` for fast chat replies and `'medium'` for day to day usage. - **Sampling**: for all reasoning efforts, we recommend the following sampling parameters: - `temperature=1.0` - `top_p=0.95` - **System Prompt**: define a clear environment and use case, including guidance on how to effectively leverage tools in agentic systems. - **Tools**: keep the set of tools well-defined and limit their number to the minimum required for the use case. - **Context**: the checkpoint supports a 1M context window. ## Breaking changes * 🚨 Separate EP logic into its own file (#49679) by @3outeille ## Quantization FP8 quantized models can now be used for adapter training (such as LoRA with PEFT). rawIngestions.contentRaw: # Release v5.21.0 ## New Model additions ### MiniCPM-OCR MiniCPM-OCR is a document-understanding model from OpenBMB's MiniCPM-V family. It keeps the MiniCPM-V 4.6 architecture, which pairs a SigLIP vision encoder and a window-attention merger with a Qwen3.5 language model. It is specialized for reading text-dense images such as scanned pages, screenshots, receipts and tables. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/minicpm_ocr) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.18154) * Feat test (#49920) by @guarin in [#49920](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49920) ### Flint Flint is Recursive's mixture-of-experts language model. Compared to a standard SwiGLU MoE transformer such as Qwen3-MoE, it uses hybrid attention (sliding-window attention with rotary embeddings over the current token and the previous 512 tokens in most layers, and full attention without positional encoding in the remaining layers). It also has learned attention sinks, as in GPT-OSS, with per-head RMS-normalized queries and keys. Each sparse layer routes a token to 6 of 256 experts by sigmoid score and adds an ungated shared expert, and the first two layers are dense. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/flint) * Add Flint model support. (#49824) by @lovishmadaan in [#49824](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49824) ### UltraVBert UltraVBert extends ModernVBert by pairing the UltraBERT text encoder with a SigLIP vision encoder for visual document understanding and retrieval. Its image processor splits each page into 512-pixel tiles plus a global view. The connector merges each 4 x 4 block of vision patches into one token, so a tile becomes 64 image tokens, and RMS-normalizes them to the scale of UltraBERT's token embeddings. The `max_image_tiles` setting (27 by default) caps the number of tiles per page. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/ultravbert) * Add UltraVBERT (#49685) by @athrael-soju in [#49685](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49685) ### Gradium Phonon TTS Gradium Phonon TTS is Gradium's family of on-device text-to-speech models, trained with the Pocket TTS recipe. A causal transformer reads a voice prompt and the text, then emits one continuous 32-dimensional audio latent per step at 12.5 Hz through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when the utterance ends. The latents are decoded to 24 kHz audio by a Pocket TTS audio tokenizer. Unlike Pocket TTS, voice conditioning uses 512-dimensional latents from a separate, unreleased speaker codec, so voices come as precomputed latents and cannot be cloned from a recording. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/gradium_phonon_tts) * Add GradiumPhononTTS (#49791) by @eustlb in [#49791](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49791) ### Pocket TTS Pocket TTS is Kyutai's 100M-parameter text-to-speech model, built as a Continuous Audio Language Model that runs faster than real time on CPU. A causal transformer emits one continuous audio latent per frame (12.5 Hz) through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when to stop. A Mimi-based audio tokenizer encodes voice prompts and decodes the generated latents to 24 kHz audio. Two flow heads are released, Lagrangian self-distillation (default) and drifting, and voices can be cloned from a recording, passed as precomputed latents, or loaded from cached KV states. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (the Continuous Audio Language Models paper, arXiv 2509.06926). It is the only paper the documentation links, and it describes the architecture family Pocket TTS belongs to. The docs do not cite a separate Pocket TTS technical report.) | [Blog Post](NONE. The documentation links no official blog post. It points only to the original code repository at https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts.) * add PocketTTS (#49589) by @eustlb in [#49589](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49589) ### Pocket TTS Audio Tokenizer The Pocket TTS audio tokenizer is the codec used by Pocket TTS. It has Mimi's architecture (SEANet convolutions plus a small causal transformer on each side), but its residual vector quantizer is replaced by a continuous 32-dimensional bottleneck, the VAE-GAN from Continuous Audio Language Models. It converts 24 kHz audio into latents at 12.5 Hz and decodes them back to audio. It serves as the `audio_tokenizer` of `PocketTTSProcessor`, encoding voice prompts and decoding generated latents, and its encoder and decoder can also be loaded on their own. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts_audio_tokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (Continuous Audio Language Models, whose VAE-GAN this tokenizer uses; arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06926)) * add PocketTTSAudioTokenizer (#49588) by @eustlb in [#49588](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49588) ## Breaking changes Fixed Gemma4 processor imports (the Gemma4, Gemma4 unified and EmbeddingGemma2 processors) so `from transformers import *` no longer fails in environments that have `PIL` but not `torch`; no user action is needed. * :rotating_light: Fix gemma4 cross imports resulting in import failing without `torch` but with `PIL` (#49748) by @Sai-Suraj-27 Added an `"fp8"` backend to `QuantizedCache`, alongside `quanto` and `hqq`, that stores KV states in `torch.float8_e4m3fn` with a single scale per tensor; enable it with `cache_implementation="quantized"` and `cache_config={"backend": "fp8"}`. * 🚨Add an FP8 backend to `QuantizedCache` (#48677) by @jiqing-feng Tensor parallelism now has a dedicated embedding style, shards every model's input embeddings by default, and supports widths that aren't divisible by the TP size, so `ColwiseParallel` and `RowwiseParallel` now apply only to linear layers; release.body: # Release v5.21.0 ## New Model additions ### MiniCPM-OCR MiniCPM-OCR is a document-understanding model from OpenBMB's MiniCPM-V family. It keeps the MiniCPM-V 4.6 architecture, which pairs a SigLIP vision encoder and a window-attention merger with a Qwen3.5 language model. It is specialized for reading text-dense images such as scanned pages, screenshots, receipts and tables. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/minicpm_ocr) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.18154) * Feat test (#49920) by @guarin in [#49920](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49920) ### Flint Flint is Recursive's mixture-of-experts language model. Compared to a standard SwiGLU MoE transformer such as Qwen3-MoE, it uses hybrid attention (sliding-window attention with rotary embeddings over the current token and the previous 512 tokens in most layers, and full attention without positional encoding in the remaining layers). It also has learned attention sinks, as in GPT-OSS, with per-head RMS-normalized queries and keys. Each sparse layer routes a token to 6 of 256 experts by sigmoid score and adds an ungated shared expert, and the first two layers are dense. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/flint) * Add Flint model support. (#49824) by @lovishmadaan in [#49824](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49824) ### UltraVBert UltraVBert extends ModernVBert by pairing the UltraBERT text encoder with a SigLIP vision encoder for visual document understanding and retrieval. Its image processor splits each page into 512-pixel tiles plus a global view. The connector merges each 4 x 4 block of vision patches into one token, so a tile becomes 64 image tokens, and RMS-normalizes them to the scale of UltraBERT's token embeddings. The `max_image_tiles` setting (27 by default) caps the number of tiles per page. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/ultravbert) * Add UltraVBERT (#49685) by @athrael-soju in [#49685](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49685) ### Gradium Phonon TTS Gradium Phonon TTS is Gradium's family of on-device text-to-speech models, trained with the Pocket TTS recipe. A causal transformer reads a voice prompt and the text, then emits one continuous 32-dimensional audio latent per step at 12.5 Hz through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when the utterance ends. The latents are decoded to 24 kHz audio by a Pocket TTS audio tokenizer. Unlike Pocket TTS, voice conditioning uses 512-dimensional latents from a separate, unreleased speaker codec, so voices come as precomputed latents and cannot be cloned from a recording. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/gradium_phonon_tts) * Add GradiumPhononTTS (#49791) by @eustlb in [#49791](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49791) ### Pocket TTS Pocket TTS is Kyutai's 100M-parameter text-to-speech model, built as a Continuous Audio Language Model that runs faster than real time on CPU. A causal transformer emits one continuous audio latent per frame (12.5 Hz) through a one-step flow head, and an end-of-speech head decides when to stop. A Mimi-based audio tokenizer encodes voice prompts and decodes the generated latents to 24 kHz audio. Two flow heads are released, Lagrangian self-distillation (default) and drifting, and voices can be cloned from a recording, passed as precomputed latents, or loaded from cached KV states. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (the Continuous Audio Language Models paper, arXiv 2509.06926). It is the only paper the documentation links, and it describes the architecture family Pocket TTS belongs to. The docs do not cite a separate Pocket TTS technical report.) | [Blog Post](NONE. The documentation links no official blog post. It points only to the original code repository at https://github.com/kyutai-labs/pocket-tts.) * add PocketTTS (#49589) by @eustlb in [#49589](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49589) ### Pocket TTS Audio Tokenizer The Pocket TTS audio tokenizer is the codec used by Pocket TTS. It has Mimi's architecture (SEANet convolutions plus a small causal transformer on each side), but its residual vector quantizer is replaced by a continuous 32-dimensional bottleneck, the VAE-GAN from Continuous Audio Language Models. It converts 24 kHz audio into latents at 12.5 Hz and decodes them back to audio. It serves as the `audio_tokenizer` of `PocketTTSProcessor`, encoding voice prompts and decoding generated latents, and its encoder and decoder can also be loaded on their own. **Links:** [Documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/pocket_tts_audio_tokenizer) | [Paper](https://huggingface.co/papers/2509.06926 (Continuous Audio Language Models, whose VAE-GAN this tokenizer uses; arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06926)) * add PocketTTSAudioTokenizer (#49588) by @eustlb in [#49588](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/49588) ## Breaking changes Fixed Gemma4 processor imports (the Gemma4, Gemma4 unified and EmbeddingGemma2 processors) so `from transformers import *` no longer fails in environments that have `PIL` but not `torch`; no user action is needed. * :rotating_light: Fix gemma4 cross imports resulting in import failing without `torch` but with `PIL` (#49748) by @Sai-Suraj-27 Added an `"fp8"` backend to `QuantizedCache`, alongside `quanto` and `hqq`, that stores KV states in `torch.float8_e4m3fn` with a single scale per tensor; enable it with `cache_implementation="quantized"` and `cache_config={"backend": "fp8"}`. * 🚨Add an FP8 backend to `QuantizedCache` (#48677) by @jiqing-feng Tensor parallelism now has a dedicated embedding style, shards every model's input embeddings by default, and supports widths that aren't divisible by the TP size, so `ColwiseParallel` and `RowwiseParallel` now apply only to linear layers; custom TP plans that applied them to embeddings must switch to the new embedding style. * 🚨 TP: give embeddings their own style, shard input embeddings by default, and shard widths that don't divide by the TP size (#49570) by @IlyasMoutawwakil Every MoE TP and EP plan now shards its experts, so models no longer keep all experts on every rank, and a new `test_moe_parallel_plans_shard_experts` test enforces this; Flash Attention now works with static caches, BLOOM no longer crashes with static cache or compiled generate, chunked prefill supports cache continuation, and the Qwen4-Exp indexer's position history stays aligned with its cached keys. ## Liquid AI LFM3

[LFM3](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3) is Liquid AI's new family of small models built for local agents, tool calling, and structured output, on Liquid's new tri-hybrid architecture. The family includes:

- [lfm3](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3): a 1.7B text model with a 256K-token context window
- [lfm3-vl](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3-vl): adds image understanding
- [lfm3-audio](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3-audio): speech recognition, translation, and text-to-speech in 18 languages
- [lfm3-omni](https://ollama.com/library/lfm3-omni): text, images, and audio in one model

```sh
ollama run lfm3
```

## d1 decision models

Liquid AI's d1 models now come in a 2B size, built on LFM3. [d1](https://ollama.com/library/d1) makes decisions about text and images, and [d1-omni](https://ollama.com/library/d1-omni) adds audio.

```sh
ollama run d1:2b "I was charged twice for order 4417." --ask "Is this a billing issue?"
```

Note: lfm3 and d1 2b are supported on Apple hardware in this release.  Support for Linux/Windows coming soon.

## What's Changed
- Faster prompt processing on Apple silicon for Gemma 4, Flint and Laguna models
- Speculative decoding now supports DFlash2 draft models on MLX
- Gemma 4 keeps more detail in small images
- `ollama launch` now works with OpenCode v2
- Fixed tool-only assistant turns from Kimi CLI
- Updated MLX and llama.cpp

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/ollama/ollama/compare/v0.40.11...v0.40.12

Ollama can now generate [speech](https://docs.ollama.com/capabilities/speech) on macOS. `ollama run` plays text or a chat model's reply aloud as the audio is generated, and apps can stream audio through the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint.

```sh
ollama run phonon "Hello from Ollama."
```

```sh
ollama run d3 "A customer says their card was charged twice." --ask "Is this a billing issue?"
```

rawIngestions.contentRaw:
Hey everyone,

ML Blocks is a node-based workflow builder to create multi-modal AI workflows without writing any code.

You connect blocks that call various visual models like GPT4v, Segment Anything, Dino etc. along with basic image processing blocks like resize, invert color, blur, crop, and several others.

The idea is to make it easier to deploy multi-step image processing workflows, without needing to spin up endless custom OpenCV cloud functions to glue together AI models. Usually, even if you're using cloud inference servers like Replicate, you still need to write your own image processing code to pre and post-process images in your pipeline. When you're trying to move fast, that's just unnecessary overhead.

With ML Blocks, you can build a workflow and deploy the whole thing as a single API. AFAIK, ML Blocks is the only end-to-end workflow builder built specifically for image processing.

If you're curious, our models run on Replicate, HuggingFace & Modal Labs cloud GPUs and we use React Flow for the node UX.
